papers.title: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement
papers.first_page: Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement De Wang Peng Qi Uniphore Uniphore de.wang@uniphore.com peng.qi@uniphore.com arXiv:2610.27465v1 [cs.AI] 20 Oct 2026 Abstract Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a deployed agent’s execution traces, derive a change, have an automated verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a platform can measure. Verifier strength σ is how well the available verifier — often an LLM judge — agrees with a trusted reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent. Recoverability is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off. Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them. We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on the platform’s own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the τ 2 -bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform’s LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9 of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome of 17% of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended only when its old version is kept and its verifier’s strength has been measured. 1 Introduction Agents built on language models now hold conversations, call tools, and write to business sys- tems (Yao et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2026). They also fail often. On the τ 2 -bench tasks we study the baseline agent solves just over half of its tasks, through ordinary mistakes: a wrong tool call, a missing confirmation, steps taken out of order (Cuadron et al., 2026). Fixing such failures means reading traces, finding the cause, revising the agent, checking the revision and deploying it. Done by hand, this does not scale with the number of agents a platform hosts, so platforms have begun to automate it (Wang et al., 2026; Li & Zhu, 2026). We call one pass of this automated repair a self-improvement step: the platform reads its own agents’ traces, derives a change, checks it with a verifier and deploys it, with no person writing the change. Inference-time self-correction (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023) and human-written fixes do not count. Training and serving became platform services long ago (Baylor et al., 2017; Moritz et al., 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). papers.title: Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners?
papers.first_page: 2026-10-20 Are Self-Evolving Agents Continual Learners? Xiaoyin Chen1,2,* , Yizheng Huang3 , Yinglun Xu3 , Ziyun Zhao3 , Emmett McQuinn3 , Julie Liu3 and Hope Yao3 1 Mila – Quebec AI Institute, 2 Université de Montréal, 3 Google DeepMind, * Work done as a student researcher at Google DeepMind Large language model agents are often deployed in environments where new knowledge, tools, and workflows keep arriving. Such an agent is therefore expected to adapt continually, learning new tasks as they arrive without forgetting earlier ones. This resembles the continual learning problem, but at a pace that conventional gradient updates cannot sustain. Nonparametric self-evolving agents are a natural alternative: they adapt by rewriting their own harness, such as prompts, memory, and skills, from task feedback while the model weights stay frozen. We study whether such agents are effective continual arXiv:2610.25858v1 [cs.AI] 19 Oct 2026 learners across four drifting task streams that shift in topic, workflow, or domain (built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld). Evaluating three representative methods spanning experience retrieval and self- modification (ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness), we find that although self-evolution improves aggregate performance on most streams, higher plasticity consistently comes at the cost of stability. Specifically, self-modifying methods apply global edits to a shared prompt or workspace, interfering with unseen tasks and overwriting earlier knowledge as the stream shifts. Conversely, similarity-based memory retrieval localizes updates across distant domains, but still retrieves foreign memories on unseen tasks and suffers from retrieval collision when similar queries require conflicting workflows. These findings show that current self-evolvin … nt that serves users over an extended period must learn each new task as it arrives while preserving what it has already learned. This form of learning resembles the classical continual learning problem, which studies how a model can be trained on new tasks over time without forgetting earlier ones (De Lange et al., 2022; Parisi et al., 2019; van de Ven and Tolias, 2019). Continual learning has recently emerged as a central challenge for LLMs (Jang et al., 2022; Ke et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2023; Shenfeld et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024). Conventionally, it has been realized through gradient updates. An LLM agent, however, is expected to adapt at the timescale of use: every interaction with the environment may yield knowledge that is useful in a later session, and that knowledge should be available as soon as the next session begins. Performing gradient updates at this pace is challenging: retraining an LLM after every session is prohibitively expensive, and fine-tuning on a small number of recent interactions is known to erode general capabilities (Luo et al., 2023). The in-context learning ability of LLMs (Brown et al., 2020; Dong et al., 2022) suggests an alternative route to adaptation. Rather than the weights, an agent can update its harness, everything wrapped around the model: the system prompt, the accumulated memory, the skill libraries, and the control code that orchestrates them. Nonparametric self-evolving agents adopt precisely this strategy, refining the harness from task outcomes and environment feedback while the weights remain frozen. Two paradigms have emerged. papers.first_page: RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process? Kaiwen Zhou1 , Udari Madhushani Sehwag1 1 Preparedness and Policy, Scale AI arXiv:2610.27735v2 [cs.AI] 21 Oct 2026 kaiwen.zhou@scale.com, prep@scale.com | https://labs.scale.com/papers/rsicontrol Abstract Recursive self-improvement, in which frontier AI models work on training the next generation, is quickly becoming a reality. However, the safety of this process has received far less attention than it should. A misaligned model training its successor can shape what that successor knows, how it behaves, and what it wants, and the harm carries forward into the next generation. We study this risk through the lens of AI control. We introduce RSI Control Arena, a testbed in which a frontier model, acting as an autonomous R&D agent, is given a benign main task from a stage of a successor model’s training pipeline together with a covert side task to install a misaligned property in the successor. The testbed contains 16 side tasks in three classes, forming 22 task pairs with main tasks that span the pipeline from data curation to reinforcement learning. We evaluate six frontier models as agents against LLM monitors that read the transcript of the run and the agent’s reasoning. We observe that every model completes a substantial share of the side tasks without degrading the main-task performance, including side tasks that make the successor itself a better saboteur. Under minimal instructions to stay covert, models already produce successful attacks that monitors fail to detect, and providing a short list of evasion tactics further reduces the detection rate. Monitors with access to agent’s reasoning detects most attacks, but not all. Our results indicate that recursive self-improvement raises significant safety concerns, and that strong safety effort should be in place before models are trusted with greater responsibility of training their successors. 1 Introduction Frontier AI models are increasingly used to build the next generation of AI models. papers.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
papers.first_page: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 353, 2026 ACML 2026 When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines Yingxin Jia jia yingxin@hotmail.com Xuanyi Li lixuanyi199801@gmail.com Independent Researchers arXiv:2610.27714v1 [cs.AI] 20 Oct 2026 Editors: Andy Song, Bo Han and Sarah Erfani Abstract When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because planners, prompts, and implementation quality vary together across systems, and the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (kinematic ob- servations, discrete meta-actions, 1 Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We freeze the planner, encoder, and protocol, treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools), and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diag- nostics, scripted certificate policies, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory TG-Mem with five vari- ants, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p = 0.011) and have a negative pool-averaged effect, and even the rulebook’s apparent pool-immunity (0.97 to 0.98 on five pools) collapsed to 0.03 to 0.98 on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler, which sits significantly above both memories under paired tests. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a scripted always-SLOWER policy and by a single 15-token caution instruction (both 0.98), and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook’s lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. Neither retrieved structure nor raw in-context history solves the oracle-solvable history-necessity diagnostic. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool compar- ison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, diagnostics with certificates, the replay benchmark, audited ports, seeds, and caches. Keywords: Large language models; autonomous driving; agent memory; temporal knowl- edge graphs; retrieval-augmented decision making; closed-loop simulation. 1. papers.first_page: Build, Don’t Play: Self-Improving LLM Research Agents Develop a Hearthstone Battlegrounds AI That Rivals Top Players Changlian Ma Limin Wang Nanjing University Nanjing University Shanghai AI Laboratory Shanghai AI Laboratory arXiv:2610.33845v1 [cs.AI] 24 Oct 2026 changlianma@smail.nju.edu.cn lmwang@nju.edu.cn Abstract Can LLM agents carry a hard real-world problem from raw data to a system that holds its own against people? We study this in Hearthstone Battlegrounds, an eight-player auto-battler with stochastic shops and battles, hidden information and nearly a thousand interacting cards. We present AUTOTAVERN, a self-improving research system: specialised LLM research agents share a typed research memory, every claim passes verification gates, and live games close the loop, so the agents improve the simulator, opponents and policy and, from the same feedback, their own research process; a human sets goals and rules on ambiguous mechanics. In 20 days AUTOTAVERN built TAVERN G YM, the first faithful, full-content reproduction of the live game, and delivered 23 versions of TAVERNAGENT, trained with PPO against opponents calibrated to real games. TAVERNAGENT plays complete games on the live ladder by itself: its rating rose from 6,000 to about 15,000 and, on the public leaderboard’s measure, its last 20 records average a placement of 1.60 with 80% first places, better than the server’s ten highest-rated players on every statistic (2.34, 59%). TAVERN B ENCH, 960 tasks in 40 scenarios, shows that the system the agents built is the strongest player: TAVERNAGENT answers 91% of the play tasks against at most 63% for frontier LLMs, and decides in 0.03 s where they need up to 26 s; within the second a live turn allows, it keeps 90% and no LLM more than 26%. LLM agents build far better than they play. We will open-source TAVERN B ENCH and TAVERN G YM at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/AutoTavern. 1 Introduction Games have long served as milestones for artificial intelligence, from Go and chess [Silver et al., 2016, 2018] to StarCraft II, Dota 2, poker, Mahjong and Stratego [Vinyals et al., 2019, Berner et al., 2019, Brown and Sandholm, 2019, Li et al., 2020, Perolat et al., 2022]. Each of these systems was the product of a large team of human experts who built the environment, designed the learning algorithm and debugged the countless ways in which a simulated training world differs from the real game. Today, LLM agents write and run much of the code behind such systems, and a growing line of work asks whether they can automate the research itself [Lu et al., 2024, Yamada et al., 2026, Wijk et al., 2025, Srikanth et al., 2026]. papers.first_page: Automating ML for Science: Can Frontier Agents Climb Scientific Hills in the Wild? Ming Zhong* 1 , Stacy Li* 1 , Nicholas Carlini 2 , Matthew Jagielski 2 1 Anthropic Fellows Program 2 Anthropic arXiv:2610.28763v1 [cs.AI] 20 Oct 2026 Abstract Frontier coding agents are increasingly framed as end-to-end automated researchers, and ML for science offers a demanding test of that promise: improving a scientific model often requires domain insight beyond routine ML engineering. We introduce AGENT 4S CI, a long-horizon testbed for measuring how far today’s agents can improve the published best models on scientific ML benchmarks, spanning 20 benchmarks across 11 domains. Rather than ranking agents on a leaderboard, AGENT 4S CI asks what kinds of progress agents can make on these tasks under in- the-wild conditions, and where they fall short. Empirically, today’s frontier agents advance the published best on every benchmark, with Claude Opus reaching 10.4% mean relative improvement and no run flagged for academic misconduct. These gains, however, come almost entirely from a bag of ML-engineering tricks rather than research-level insight. Trajectory analysis surfaces three recurring limitations in this setting: novelty miscalibration, resource under-utilization, and rapid collapse into local engineering sweeps. Lightweight plug-in skills for research ideation, experiment management, and scheduled checklists raise Claude Opus from 10.4% to 20.1% and Codex from 4.4% to 8.1%, while yielding more diverse, domain- relevant interventions. AGENT 4S CI gives the community a way to track and push frontier agents from ML engineering toward domain insight on real-world ML-for- science problems. Code and data are available on GitHub and Hugging Face. 1 Introduction Recent advances in frontier coding agents are turning automated research into an executable workflow: agents can read papers and repositories, modify implementations, run experiments, interpret quantita- tive feedback, and iterate. A growing body of recent work suggests a common recipe for this vision: cast research as a feedback loop in which an agent operates in a workspace, pursues a measurable objective, and improves through experimentation [50, 38, 28, 62, 23]. Yet most demonstrations so far assume well-structured codebases [19, 36, 61], operate in single-task settings [50, 38, 23], and are heavily skewed toward computer science domains [40, 56, 13]. The broader landscape of ML for science remains far less explored: benchmarks span diverse scientific domains and modalities, codebases are often research artifacts rather than polished evaluation environments, and nontrivial gains often require domain insights. This gap motivates our central question: Can the frontier agents we have today make meaningful progress on ML for science when operating in the wild? We instantiate this question as automated scientific hill-climbing (Figure 1). In this setting, an agent is given a scientific ML benchmark, its paper, codebase, data, and target metric. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model’s behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines, and record dollar-denominated inference cost as a practical resource measure. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revi- sions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [−1.44, 7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. Human-steered systems demon- strate further headroom, although their development and selection procedures differ. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities. 1 I NTRODUCTION Modern language models can write programs, call tools, and act in unfamiliar environments, but only as part of a larger agentic system. In such a system, a symbolic program orchestrates calls to the model, shaping what it observes, what it retains, which actions are available, how it recovers from failure, and how much inference it spends. This surrounding system is commonly termed a harness (Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026a). A system’s behavior therefore depends on both its harness and its underlying model or models. This matters for the study of general intelligence, which requires the efficient acquisition of useful new skills in unfamiliar situations (Chollet, 2019). If each novel task requires a human engineer to inspect failures, redesign representations, add tools, and tune control flow, then what improves is not the system’s own capacity to adapt but the engineer’s understanding, transferred into the system by hand. The agent’s learning remains confined to a supplied mechanism whose improvement depends on the engineer. In contrast, humans routinely adapt to unfamiliar situations in everyday life. ∗ Work done outside of Amazon. 1

papers.first_page: OptScientist: Automated Discovery of Optimization Laws Ma ZhenYao∗ 1,2 , Yue Liang1,3 , and Jian-Qiao Zhu4 1 Plokerm AI Lab 2 Xiamen University 3 University of Tübingen arXiv:2610.28562v1 [cs.AI] 20 Oct 2026 4 The University of Hong Kong Abstract Many scientific phenomena are best understood as outcomes of underlying op- timization problems, yet automated scientific discovery has largely focused on recovering equations that describe observed input–output patterns. We introduce OptScientist, a novel automated framework for discovering compact symbolic optimization laws directly from data. OptScientist comprises (i) a model that infers symbolic optimization problems by first learning to represent data as an optimization problem and then extracting its symbolic form, and (ii) an LLM agen- tic system embedding the model in a discovery process that integrates theoretical priors from scientific literature, discovers candidate laws, abstracts their underlying mechanisms, and suggests new data to collect. We first evaluate OptScientist on OptFeynman, a novel benchmark of 99 physics-derived optimization problems, where OptScientist recovers ground-truth laws for over 80% of the problems and remains robust to noisy contextual information, while substantially outperforming machine-learning, symbolic, and LLM-based model-discovery baselines. On hu- man risky choice and central-bank monetary policy, OptScientist discovers compact symbolic optimization laws that achieve held-out predictive performance compet- itive with leading baselines, while using few parameters and substantially fewer tokens than LLM baselines. Overall, OptScientist extends automated scientific discovery to uncovering optimization laws that generate observed phenomena, enabling automated theory building across the physical, biological, behavioral, and social sciences. 1 Introduction Across the sciences, many influential theories characterize observed phenomena as solutions to optimization problems. Examples include energy or free-energy minimization principles for charac- terizing equilibrium states in statistical physics (Gibbs, 1902; Landau & Lifshitz, 2013), optimality models for explaining how biological fitness shapes evolutionary outcomes (Wright et al., 1932; Fisher, 1999), rational and resource-rational analyses of human behavior and cognition (Samuelson, 1948; Debreu, 1959; Anderson, 1991; Lieder & Griffiths, 2020), and intertemporal optimization for modelling dynamic macroeconomic systems (Ramsey, 1928; Ljungqvist & Sargent, 2018). Devel- oping such theories requires identifying objectives and relevant constraints that jointly account for observed outcomes. However, these components are typically formulated by domain experts and only subsequently evaluated against data, making optimization-based theory construction largely manual and dependent on specialized insight. This reliance on expert formulation creates a substantial bottleneck for theory discovery across scientific domains. A fundamental question therefore remains: Can optimization laws be discovered automatically from observational data? ∗ Corresponding author: zhenyaoma@163.com

As these empirical principles are often unknown in complex discovery processes, they are constructed via a hypotheses-to-principle pipeline to obtain recurring causalities from progressively accumulated observations during test-time discovery. However, constructing this knowledge requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, making this translation stage a bottleneck for scientific discovery. To address this limitation, we propose P RINCIPIA, an LLM-based framework that constructs and continu- ally refines scientific principles at test-time. Drawing on how human researchers develop principles, P RINCIPIA forms comparative causal hypotheses from related inputs and their observed outcomes, then synthesizes recurring relationships across these hypotheses into inductive principles. By applying the constructed hypotheses and inductive principles to the task, it obtains new observations, revises the used hypotheses based on these new observations, and reconstructs principles from the updated hypotheses, allowing scientific knowledge to continuously evolve through- out test-time discovery. Across benchmarks spanning molecular optimization, protein engineering, gene perturbation, and molecular property prediction, P RIN - CIPIA outperforms baselines relying on internal knowledge, external sources, or experience summaries, w … ific discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/DongkiKim95/Principia. 1 I NTRODUCTION Scientific discovery has long driven human progress, enabling advances across chemistry, biology, and medicine. Central to this process is identifying scientific principles that govern the systems of interest. In complex scientific discovery processes such as drug discovery, the scientific principles are usually unknown due to the complexity of the underlying systems. Therefore, empirical principles are usually constructed from progressively accumulated experimental observations during test-time discovery to explain causality between input characteristics and experimental outcomes (Scheiner & Willig, 2008; Hone et al., 2015; Pearlstein et al., 2021). Specifically, hypotheses that explain a specific scope of individual observations are formed and then generalized into principles that cover a broader scope of observations, being formulated as a hypotheses-to-principle construction pipeline (Lamma et al., 2000; Kakas & Michael, 2020; Engelschalt et al., 2023). However, constructing such principles by human researchers requires substantial domain expertise, time, and effort, creating a bottleneck in scientific discovery. As illustrated in Fig. 1, human re- searchers also follow the hypotheses-to-principle construction pipeline, while leveraging an extensive body of prior knowledge. They interpret the experimental observations, hypothesize the plausible causal relationships, generalize them by analyzing the recurring patterns, and revise hypotheses when new observations contradict prior explanations. papers.title: MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research
papers.first_page: MatOS: An Agent Operating System for Materials Research AI Materials Team Zhongguancun Academy · Zhongguancun Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Beijing, China Team e-mail: aimaterials@bza.edu.cn arXiv:2610.34203v1 [cs.AI] 25 Oct 2026 Abstract Materials research relies on data, knowledge, and simulation tools that are scattered across many sources and continue to grow. A single study often involves multi-day workflows that it- erate between literature analysis, computation, and experiment. Large language model (LLM) agents have made rapid progress in this setting: they can retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and, when coupled with autonomous laboratories, close design–synthesis– characterization loops. However, in materials research, extending these agents with new capa- bilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and enabling them to evolve by learning from past tasks and user feedback remain diﬀicult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research built on three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets that agents can combine and extend for new tasks; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs research tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that long-running tasks can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback, so that experience gained in one task can be reused in later ones. On ResearchClawBench, MatOS improves on the previously best-performing agent by 11.15% with the same base model and extends the cost–score Pareto frontier. With a common base model, MatOS also achieves higher success rates than Codex CLI and Claude Code, exceeding Codex CLI by 2.13% on MatTools and by 4.17% on SciAgentGym. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, and linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to specific local atomic environments. It also supported the development of two new methods: a training-data se- lection strategy that reduces interatomic-potential errors by 3.1% relative to DIRECT at the same data budget, and an alloy melting-temperature model with 13.6% lower error than the best baseline. Together, these results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies reliably, from large-scale screening to the development of new methods. papers.title: Auditing the Product, Not the Recursion: The Evaluation Evidence Behind Recursive Self-Improvement Claims
papers.first_page: AUDITING THE P RODUCT, N OT THE R ECURSION : T HE E VALUATION E VIDENCE B EHIND R ECURSIVE S ELF -I MPROVEMENT C LAIMS Zihan Chen Di Zhu Lei Nico Zheng Stevens Institute of Technology Stevens Institute of Technology University of Massachusetts Boston arXiv:2610.27610v1 [cs.LG] 20 Oct 2026 Hoboken, NJ, USA Hoboken, NJ, USA Boston, MA, USA zchen61@stevens.edu dzhu1@stevens.edu lei.zheng@umb.edu A BSTRACT Recursive self-improvement (RSI) promises AI systems, such as self-evolving LLM agents, that become better at producing further improvements. Evaluating this promise requires separating product claims about the final system from process claims about the improvement process itself. Existing surveys specify the evidence these claims require, but how often studies report that evidence remains unmeasured. We examine this question through full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, including 90 that describe their own systems as RSI. The codebook links claims to evaluation designs. Independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and a separate blind coding of improver comparisons assess coding reliability. Among the 90 RSI studies, 90% report product evaluation beyond development tasks under a broad criterion that includes partial or unstated separation, while 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection. Only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. In a human-coded random sample, the RSI studies show the same contrast: 45% evaluate on tasks unused for selection and 14% audit two or more reruns. Of the 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, 23 report a related comparison, but only 4 compare earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. Across these results and a comparison set of established works, evidence for repeatability and improved procedures remains less developed than product evaluation. Three propositions explain how selection effects, shared evaluator errors, and changes in system state limit what product evaluations can establish. Together, the findings support a claim-indexed reporting standard that connects each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it. Keywords recursive self-improvement (RSI) · self-evolving agents · LLM agents · evaluation methodology · meta-research · LLM-as-a-judge 1 Introduction Language models increasingly participate in the processes that improve AI systems. They revise prompts and agent harnesses, which coordinate a model’s tools and actions [1–4]. They also generate feedback for updating model weights [5–7] and modify data and training pipelines [8, 9]. Some systems also modify the procedure that proposes changes, which we call the improver, or the evaluator that decides which changes to retain [10–14]. These developments motivate the ambition of recursive self-improvement (RSI): retained improvements should enable the system to produce further improvements, potentially by making the improver itself more effective. This ambition creates an evaluation problem. A higher final benchmark score establishes something about the resulting system, but it does not by itself establish how the improvement process behaves. Whether gains accumulate across rounds, recur in independent runs, or result from a better improver are distinct empirical questions. We refer to these as process claims, in contrast to a product claim about the performance of the final system. Evaluating RSI requires matching the evidence to the particular claim being made.

papers.title: CoMem: Learning to Anticipate Failures from Retrieved Experience
papers.first_page: Preprint C O M EM : L EARNING TO A NTICIPATE FAILURES FROM R ETRIEVED E XPERIENCE Yun Shen1 Ming Shen2,3 Tianjun Yao2,* 1 2 3 The Ohio State University Shenzhen Loop Area Institute Shanghai Jiaotong University * Corresponding author. A BSTRACT arXiv:2610.25790v1 [cs.CL] 19 Oct 2026 Reflection lets LLM agents improve from their own attempts, but the memory it builds is local to a single task, so an agent reflecting on its own tends to revisit the same explanation for failure. Cross-task reflective memory addresses this in two forms: retrieved memory keeps past experience explicit and looks up related cases, which is specific but bounded by the bank, and parametric memory inter- nalizes experience into parameters, which generalizes but is grounded in nothing beyond the task description. When both are used, existing agents combine them additively, feeding their outputs to the solver side by side, so retrieved experience never changes what the learned memory produces. We introduce CoMem (Com- pounding Memory), which makes retrieved experience an input to the learned memory itself, at training and at inference. The agent builds a bank of its own successful and failed reflections, learns from retrieved cases to write failure hy- potheses, candidate explanations of how an attempt is likely to go wrong, and at test time reasons from newly retrieved cases to guide each attempt. Varying the retrieved cases gives the memory different perspectives, yielding reflective diver- sity that is not merely sampled but also grounded in retrieved experience. Across two backbones and five benchmarks in math, code, and multi-hop QA, CoMem achieves strong overall performance. Additional evaluations show that it gener- alizes to out-of-distribution tasks and enables smaller models to provide eff … ather than from a stronger external model (Zelikman et al., 2022; Madaan et al., 2023). At test time, the dominant mechanism for such improvement is reflection, in which the agent verbalizes what went wrong after a failed attempt and carries this guidance into the next trial (Shinn et al., 2023). Reflection-based frameworks have become a standard component of language agents for programming, mathematical reasoning, and multi-hop question answering (Yao et al., 2023b; Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). The effectiveness of reflection, however, is bounded by its diversity. Studies of self-correction report that a model left to reflect on its own tends to produce repetitive or superficial diagnoses that miss the actual cause of failure (Huang et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024), so later attempts revisit the same explanation instead of exploring alternative ones. Conversely, more diverse reflections correlate strongly with higher task success (Lingam et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026). Existing work introduces diversity by varying prompts and sampling (Lingam et al., 2025), searching over multiple reasoning branches (Yao et al., 2023a; Zhou et al., 2024), retrieving trajectories of previously solved tasks from a cross-sample memory bank (Lingam et al., 2025), and, most recently, training a lightweight para- metric memory that generates reflective signals from patterns internalized across many tasks (Yao et al., 2026). The latter two are notable because they let an agent draw on experience beyond the current task, and both can be built entirely from the base model’s own trajectories. papers.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
papers.first_page: ExpEvolve ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery Yongqiang Chen*†1,2 , Chenxi Liu*3 , Deyu Zou*4 , Zhenhao Chen1 , Tongliang Liu5,1 , Bo Han3 and Kun Zhang1,2 1 MBZUAI, 2 Carnegie Mellon University, 3 TMLR Group, Hong Kong Baptist University, 4 The Chinese University of Hong Kong, 5 SAIC Centre, The University of Sydney * Core contributors. † Project lead. yqchen24@gmail.com Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language arXiv:2610.29303v1 [cs.LG] 21 Oct 2026 Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0×. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery. 1. Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used to build agents that operate on increasingly long- horizon tasks (Plaat et al., 2025). One of the most ambitious applications is AI scientist agents (Zheng et al., 2025a), in which LLMs automate the scientific discovery process, including literature sur- veys (Asai et al., 2026), hypothesis generation (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024), data-driven analysis (Majumder et al., 2025), experiment design (Li et al., 2025a), or even the whole discov- ery workflow (Gottweis et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2024; Mitchener et al., 2025; Yamada et al., 2025). LLM-driven discovery has shown strong results in a variety of domains, such as mathematics (Ope- nAI, 2026b,c), de novo protein design (Anthropic, 2026), algorithm discovery (Lange et al., 2026; Novikov et al., 2025), and the research that develops LLMs themselves, an early form of recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Favaro and Clark, 2026; Karpathy, 2026; Lyu et al., 2026a; OpenAI, 2026a). At the heart of the discovery loop is the iteration over scientific hypotheses, where scientific ideas compound throughout the evaluation of promising hypotheses (Wallace et al., 2026). Therefore, it is essential to reuse the discovery experience to generate high-quality hypotheses, e.g., avoiding getting stuck in repetitive mistakes or suboptimal solutions and encoding promising exploratory proposals. In this work, we study experience reuse in open-ended discovery with evolutionary coding agents, where hypotheses are represented as solution programs to the underlying scientific problem, and expe- riences are accumulated as evaluated programs and their scores given by an explicit evaluator (Novikov et al., 2025). papers.title: MTA-Zero: Self-Improving Multimodal Deep Search via Online QA-Solver Co-training
papers.first_page: MTA-Z E R O : S ELF -I MPROVING M ULTIMODAL D EEP S EARCH VIA O NLINE QA–S OLVER C O - TRAINING Xiangyu Peng, Jiaxin Zhang, An Yan, Yu Li Ran Xu, Zeyuan Chen, Chien-Sheng Wu becky.peng@salesforce.com A BSTRACT arXiv:2610.33799v1 [cs.CL] 24 Oct 2026 Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong visual reason- ers, yet remain limited in open-world, multi-step search that requires grounding images, selecting tools, and integrating web evidence. Existing approaches typi- cally construct and filter fixed offline corpora whose question distributions cannot adapt as the target deep-search agent improves. Building on MTA-Agent’s image- grounded QA construction (Peng et al., 2026), we present MTA-Zero, an on- line multimodal QA–Solver co-training framework for self-improving multimodal deep-search agents that requires no precomputed multi-hop corpus. Starting from image-grounded VQA seed contexts, a trainable QA Generator retrieves evidence and constructs verified multi-hop questions online. A separate deep-search Solver then selects tools, gathers evidence, and answers the generated questions. To fo- cus generation on the Solver’s learning frontier, we derive a Goldilocks reward for the QA Generator from the Solver’s group-wise rollout success rate: questions solved by all rollouts or by none receive zero reward, whereas questions near the current frontier are favored. We optimize the two policies independently with GRPO, without sharing parameters or gradients. Across six multimodal deep- search benchmarks, MTA-Zero improves a Qwen3-VL-8B Solver from 36.91% to 51.58% mean accuracy and achieves performance comparable to GPT-5 under the same agent workflow. The same framework also improves a newer Qwen3.6- 27B Solver by 10.82 points. These results show that verified online question generation provides a policy-specific curriculum for continually improving multi- modal deep-search agents. 1 I NTRODUCTION Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made substantial progress in visual understand- ing and reasoning (Xue et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Qwen-Team, 2025). Yet, turning them into open-world agents that can identify entities in images, gather web evidence, and compose multi-hop answers through external tools remains challenging (Geng et al., 2025; Chng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). Improving a target multimodal deep-search agent remains an open problem. We refer to this deployment-time agent as the Solver agent. The Solver must learn not only to reason over an image, but also to decide what to search for, which tools to invoke, and how to integrate evidence collected across modalities. A dominant approach is to improve multimodal deep-search agents through an offline data factory (Peng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Yao et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Starting from seed images or questions, capable models and tools synthesize candidate multi-hop QA pairs and search trajec- tories; verification and filtering then turn them into SFT or RL corpora such as MTA-Agent (Peng et al., 2026), MM-DeepResearch (Yao et al., 2026), and REDSearcher (Chu et al., 2026). These pipelines create valuable, broadly reusable datasets, but their question distributions are fixed before the target Solver begins to evolve. As the Solver evolves, a generic question may be unanswerable at an early stage, trivial at a later one, or simply unrelated to its current capability gaps. Consequently, a fixed offline corpus may devote much of its generation, verification, and tool-interaction workload to questions that are no longer informative for the evolving policy. 1

papers.title: PACE: Research Proving Agent for Adaptive Conjecture Exploration
papers.first_page: PACE: Research Proving Agent for Adaptive Conjecture Exploration Shu Miao1,* Feiming Wang2,* Wentao Long3 Chenyi Li1 Kun Yuan1 Zaiwen Wen1,† 1 2 3 Peking University Nankai University Fudan University Abstract arXiv:2610.33690v1 [cs.AI] 24 Oct 2026 Many mathematical research agents focus on solving problems with fixed statements. However, conjecture research, especially in applied mathematics, may require revising candidate questions or conclusions as investigation proceeds, coupling problem formulation with proof development. We present PACE, a research–proof agent that supports this process through a structured research loop that selects mathematical objectives and develops or challenges candidate mechanisms. The whole prover constructs proofs from these mechanisms, and an independent verifier checks them against the original target. Evidence-tracking memory stores assumptions and dependencies arising during research and marks evidence for revalidation when a candidate or condition changes. This memory supports task-specific context composition that keeps checked premises, exploratory material and unresolved obligations distinct. To evaluate proof construction and conjecture research, we introduce ResearchProofBench, an applied- mathematics benchmark focused on optimization, comprising 51 known-proof tasks with 331 hidden checkpoints under historical abstract access and six open-problem cases. The known-proof tasks assess reconstruction of published results, while the open-problem cases assess mathematical investigation and proof development. On the 51 known-proof tasks, PACE achieves an aggregate Proof Score of 75.16 and completes 20 proofs. In conjecture research, PACE develops conditional results, with its submissions receiving higher review scores than the compared … ver uses retrieved or supplied definitions and theorems to guide stepwise and complete proof generation (Welleck et al., 2021; 2022). papers.title: From Prose to Properties: Testing Research Claims with ARATest for Agent-Native Science
papers.first_page: ARA Lab From Prose to Properties: Testing Research Claims with ARATest for Agent-Native Science Yifeng He1, 2 , Jiachen Liu2 , Hao Chen3 1 University of California, Davis, 2 ARA Lab, 3 The University of Hong Kong AI agents now run experiments and report findings, so research produces claims faster than researchers can check them. Each empirical claim implies a property that must hold over its cases, but it states arXiv:2610.30495v1 [cs.AI] 21 Oct 2026 that property only in prose. Without an explicit property, no test can decide which evidence would falsify a claim, so validation cannot keep pace with the claims agents produce. To make claims testable, we approximate a claim’s semantics by abstracting its property skeleton, a parameterized relation that recurs across claims. We present ARATest, a property-based testing library that checks these skeletons as executable tests. A typed declaration binds a claim to a skeleton and fixes the claim’s compared quantities, cases, scope, and numerical policy. A shared case type makes every generator supply cases in the claim’s statistical unit. A three-valued semantics assigns each property one of three verdicts: holds, violated, or inconclusive. Every violation carries a replayable witness. A default generator reads the evidence that agent-native research artifacts (ARA) link to each claim, and auto-research generators dispatch an agent to run released code for fresh cases. Our DissClaimer plugin supplies that agent and runs these generators as continuous testing. Of 243 claims in 33 existing ARA artifacts, 54 received a faithful declaration bound to evidence. ARATest decided 40 of them: 32 held and eight were violated, and the other 14 remained inconclusive. Two violations exposed errors in published papers; we found no prior report of either, and the authors of both papers confirmed them. In each, the prose contradicts the paper’s own table. ARATest detected all 553 seeded faults in reported tables without a false alarm on 19 valid controls, whereas two LLM judges given the same evidence detected 342 and 319. On fresh runs of released code from two peer-reviewed papers, four of six tests held, and the other two exposed behaviors that the reported evidence could not show. In DissClaimer campaigns on three of the 33 artifacts, six of 11 checks held and none was violated. These results suggest that once a claim’s property is explicit, one fixed test can check the claim against both reported and fresh evidence and catch errors that LLM judges miss. Code: https://github.com/ARA-Labs/aratest 1 Introduction Over the past two decades, high-level languages and open-source libraries made writing a program cheap, so the bottleneck shifted from producing software to establishing that it is correct [27]. AI agents now bring the same shift to research, the other half of the research and development cycle. They design experiments, run them, and report results [17, 21, 1], and even use those results to improve themselves [15, 13]. OpenAI [37] reported 3.1 agent-workdays of runtime for every workday of human research labor, and venue submissions keep growing [25]. Once producing a result stops being the bottleneck, deciding which results justify the next step becomes one. That decision requires validating each claim against its evidence. But a claim states the property it implies only in prose, so automated validation falls to LLM judges that read the prose [55]. This check is unsound and scales poorly: LLM judges are slow and costly, and the same evidence can pass on one run and fail on the next [46, 42]. Correspondence: Yifeng He (yfhe.cs@gmail.com) 1

papers.title: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting
papers.first_page: Evolving with Open Worlds: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Future Forecasting § § Zhipeng Chen1,2* , Yunsen Liang1,2* , Yanxi Chen1 , Hongkang Zhao1 , Lingyun Feng1 , § Ruiyang Ren3 , Guoxin Chen1 , Jia Deng1,2 , Feng Chang2 , Chuan Hao2 , Ran Tao2 , Jian Yang2 , Ji-Rong Wen1† , Bryan Dai2† , Wayne Xin Zhao1† 1 Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China 2 IQuest Research 3 Nanyang Technological University * Equal contributors † Corresponding Authors § Work done during an internship at IQuest Research. Email: {zhipeng_chen,yunsenliang04,jrwen}@ruc.edu.cn, arXiv:2610.29784v2 [cs.CL] 22 Oct 2026 batmanfly@gmail.com Abstract Most contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) systems are released with frozen parameters and improve through external updates, whereas an ideal system would keep improving from its own experience, a capacity we call recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet studying RSI requires an environment that is continuously changing, objectively verifiable, and naturally grounded, posing a fundamental challenge for agent evolution. Here we introduce E VO F O R E S I G H T , a sustainable evolution agent system grounded in future event prediction, in which agents continuously interact with a dynamically evolving environment and improve by internalizing and externalizing the experience gained through these interactions. A living environment synthesizes verifiable tasks, and a recursive-evolution engine turns the reasoning trajectory behind each prediction back into capability: decoupling search from prediction adapts parameter-level evolution to the contamination-prone live environment, while distilling reusable skills lets the agent evolve from the limited live trajectories such an environment affords. On the FutureX leaderboard, which evaluates predictions against real-world outcomes and is updated weekly, our self-improved forecaster ranked first across all systems over three consecutive weeks, achieving up to a 195% improvement in rating. On our synthesized evaluation, it ranked among the top three across four base LLMs, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 10.7 Bradley–Terry points. More broadly, these results suggest that a system built for self-improvement is best understood as an agent that co-evolves with a genuinely living, open- ended environment, pointing to a shift in AI from training static models on fixed data toward cultivating agents that grow stronger from their own experience, with such an open world as the indispensable basis of that growth. Our resources are available at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/EvoForesight. 1. Introduction Intelligence is often measured by what a system can do at a single moment in time [2, 19]. papers.title: Holding a Steady Course: Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons for Continual Agent Learning
papers.first_page: Holding a Steady Course: Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons for Continual Agent Learning Wenzhe Fan1 ∗ † Benjamin Steenhoek2 Gaurav Mittal2 Yu Hu2 1 2 University of Illinois Chicago, IL, USA Microsoft, Redmond, WA, USA arXiv:2610.34043v1 [cs.LG] 25 Oct 2026 Abstract Autonomous agents are increasingly deployed across sequences of related tasks, yet they often fail to retain and improve their knowledge over time. Existing approaches convert interaction trajectories into memories or reusable skills, but experience is not automatically reliable knowledge. Automatically collected skills and memories can propagate errors, mislead, and corrupt useful knowledge. To address this gap, we introduce Knowledge Evolution from Expertise and Lessons (KEEL), an agent-agnostic framework that uses verifier evidence to transform successful behavior into reusable skills and failures into corrective lessons. As new evidence accumulates, individual skill claims can be supported, contradicted, replaced, or retired. On SkillFlow benchmark, KEEL improves task success by 4.2 to 21.7 percentage points over the no-knowledge baseline, compared with gains of 2.4 to 9.6 points from SkillFlow’s default method. Ablations show that skills and lessons are complementary. These results show that reliable continual agent learning depends not simply on accumulating experience, but on continually validating and evolving the knowledge derived from it. Our code is available at: https://github.com/microsoft/KEEL-TTCL26. 1 Introduction Large language model agents increasingly perform complex tasks across diverse domains [1, 2]. Yet most agents are commonly developed and evaluated in static episodic settings due to the challenges of enacting realistic multi-turn/multi-session evaluations [3]. As a result, when applied in a lifelong learning scenario, where an agent is repeatedly applied for different tasks in a given project or group of projects, agents commonly fail to persist knowledge between tasks [4, 5]. A growing body of work enables agents to improve from experience without updating the parameters of their underlying language models. These include methods for distilling interactions into reusable natural-language text [6, 7], creating executable and reusable skill libraries [8–10], and combining the two approaches to maintain complementary representation of individual experiences and higher-level skills [4, 11–14]. Recent methods further improve skill reliability through additional validation executions [15], or combine repeated skill evaluation with policy optimization [16, 17]. While these studies demonstrate that persisted knowledge can support improvement across interac- tions, they suffer from a critical limitation: experience is not automatically reliable knowledge. In particular, a successful task outcome does not guarantee that the underlying trajectory contains reliable behavior [18]. An interaction trajectory may interleave useful behavior with ineffective or harmful actions, and may satisfy some verifier checks while violating others. Starting from a fixed initial model, an agent curates post-training data for five domains over repeated rounds. In each round the current principles direct which datasets the agent searches for and pulls from HuggingFace, and which entries it keeps; the resulting entries are committed to a persistent pool, which is submitted for fine-tuning and tested on the per-domain benchmarks; the scores are then used to update the principles for the next round. papers.title: Continual Learning Exam: Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents
papers.first_page: Continual Learning Exam Benchmarking Long-Horizon RSI and Experiential Learning in LLM Agents CLE Team Continual learning is the ability of LLM agents to improve over time by acquiring, refining, and applying knowledge from experience while retaining useful prior knowledge. It is essential for agents learning over long time horizons, yet current evaluations largely assess individual task performance rather than improve- ment through accumulated experience. We introduce Continual Learning Exam (CLE), a large-scale bench- mark developed by 50+ domain experts to measure experience-driven improvement in realistic professional workflows. CLE comprises 120 human-authored tasks, each organised as a five-level ladder, yielding 600 levels spanning 89 professional roles across 12 occupational domains. Agents must pass each level to unlock the next, with later levels building on experience accumulated during earlier assignments. An evaluation agent assesses each submission against human-authored rubrics. We compare a single-submission setting with one that provides diagnostic feedback after failure and allows one revision. Across 17 harness–model arXiv:2610.33956v1 [cs.LG] 25 Oct 2026 configurations using frontier LLMs, feedback and revision yield a median completion gain of 5.3 percentage points. Yet the best-performing system clears only 47.7% of levels and completes all five levels in just 23.3% of tasks, highlighting the difficulty of sustained learning from experience for existing frontier LLMs. As such, the dataset can also be used to post-train LLMs to strengthen their continual learning capabilities.  Homepage: https://haoyu-zhao.github.io/CLE/ Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/Continual-Learning-Exam § GitHub: https://github.com/haoyu-zhao/Continual-Learning-Exam # Co … & 2 · 600 Levels Median +5.3 pp Harness / Model Trial 2 (%) Harness / Model Gain (pp) Claude Code / Opus 5 47.7 Claude Code / Sonnet 5 +13.2 Claude Code / Sonnet 5 40.2 Hermes / Doubao-Seed-Evolving +9.7 Hermes / Gemini 3.7 Flash 33.7 Hermes / Gemini 3.7 Flash +8.3 Codex / GPT-5.6-Sol 33.2 Hermes / Hy3 +7.0 Codex / GPT-5.6-Terra 33.2 OpenClaw / Doubao-Seed-Evolving +6.7 Hermes / Doubao-Seed-Evolving 30.0 Claude Code / Opus 5 +5.5 Hermes / Hy3 27.3 Hermes / DeepSeek V4 Pro +5.5 Hermes / DeepSeek V4 Pro 27.3 Codex / GPT-5.6-Sol +5.3 Hermes / Qwen3.8-Max 26.7 Codex / GPT-5.6-Terra +5.3 Codex / GPT-5.6-Luna 25.3 OpenClaw / Gemini 3.7 Flash +5.3 Hermes / GLM 5.3 24.0 OpenClaw / GLM 5.3 +5.3 OpenClaw / Gemini 3.7 Flash 24.0 Codex / GPT-5.6-Luna +5.0 OpenClaw / Doubao-Seed-Evolving 21.2 OpenClaw / Hy3 +4.2 OpenClaw / Qwen3.8-Max 19.8 OpenClaw / Qwen3.8-Max +1.7 OpenClaw / Hy3 14.0 Hermes / GLM 5.3 +1.5 OpenClaw / GLM 5.3 11.5 Hermes / Qwen3.8-Max +1.0 OpenClaw / DeepSeek V4 Pro 10.0 OpenClaw / DeepSeek V4 Pro -1.3 0 10 20 30 40 50 0 5 10 15 Completion (%) Trial 2 − Trial 1 (pp) Trial 1 Increase Decrease Figure 1: CLE at a Glance. papers.title: RSI-Opt: Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents For Model Training
papers.first_page: RSI-Opt: Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents For Model Training Binghang Lu1,∗ , Yige Sun2 , Guang Lin1,∗ 1 Purdue University 2 Independent Researcher ∗ Corresponding authors arXiv:2610.32026v1 [cs.AI] 23 Oct 2026 Abstract Conventional neural-network training typically follows a predefined optimization recipe, motivating a LLM agent that monitors training dynamics and adjusts optimizer settings as training progresses, but a fixed agent policy does not accumulate experience across runs. We introduce RSI-Opt, a plug-and-play Recursive Self-Improvement Optimizer Agents which evolves the knowledge that guides this process: a prompt, a playbook of procedures, a library of tested optimizer code, and a decision cadence. A meta-agent rewrites this policy using evidence from earlier runs, and an archive retains evaluated policies for further evolution. Across 5 generations on three training tasks, the meta-agents develop reusable procedures and code and conduct their own CPU proxy experiments. RSI-Opt substantially improves optimizer-agent performance, with representative raw-space summary z-scores increasing from +10.48 to +14.33 on the evolution suite with Opus 5.5 and from −0.36 to +3.11 on held-out tasks with GPT-5.5 through cross-model policy transfer. On the Burgers PDE, it reduces mean relative L2 error by approximately 2.7-fold with Opus 5.5 and 8.8-fold with GPT-6.1 over the fixed-prompt agent baseline, although PDE transfer varies across LLMs and tasks. Controlled comparisons show that the evolved policy combines reusable optimization knowledge with adaptation to each task: initial decisions capture most observed gains on seen tasks, while continued adaptation improves outcomes on unseen tasks. These findings demonstrate how procedures and executable tools accumulated across training runs can improve optimizer-agent performance and support transfer to scientific machine learning. 1 Introduction Neural-network training usually begins with an optimizer and schedule chosen in advance. Their effectiveness can depend on the architecture, data, and training dynamics, yet selecting a new recipe often requires repeated runs and manual intervention. A coding agent offers another form of adaptation: it can inspect a training run and revise the optimizer’s program while the model trains. Concurrent work on reactive optimizers, OPAL [2], studies this within-run setting. A single LLM agent observes training dynamics and revises the update rule, learning rates, schedules, and diagnostics during an individual run. Its conversation persists within that run, but its fixed initial policy does not retain lessons for the next one. A useful optimizer change, a misleading diagnostic, or a tested implementation must be rediscovered when a new run starts.We study whether optimizer agents can improve this initial policy across runs through recursive self-improvement.
